sections.heading: Who actually teaches Theory of Knowledge in a Ras Al Khaimah school
paragraphs: Ask the question directly at the next parents' evening, because the answer shapes everything else. In most Ras Al Khaimah IB campuses, TOK is coordinated by a teacher whose main job is a subject — often English, History or a science — and delivered either in a timetabled slot or in blocks spread through the year. Some campuses share the teaching across several subject staff so that students meet different areas of knowledge from people who work in them. Both models can be good. What neither model gives is a department with spare capacity.

The practical consequences are specific. There is usually one person who can tell a student whether their exhibition object will work, and that person is marking the whole cohort's exhibitions. There is usually one person who has read all six prescribed titles closely, and that person is also writing predicted grades for a subject class. When a student needs a second opinion in the week before a draft deadline, the queue is short but the capacity is shorter.

This is where an external coach earns their place in a small emirate, and it is worth being precise about what the role is. The school owns the assessment: it sets the internal deadlines, marks the exhibition, authenticates the work and submits it. An external tutor's job is to make the student better at the thinking, to question a weak argument before the school sees it, and to be available on a Tuesday evening when the coordinator is not. It is not to run a parallel TOK course.

There is one route that should not be taken. Professional-ethics rules in some emirates prohibit school staff from paid private tutoring of students enrolled at their own school, and the MoHRE private tuition work permit carries a code of conduct barring the same thing. Paying your child's own TOK coordinator for evening sessions is the one option on this page to rule out, and the school will confirm its own position if asked.

sections.heading: What the Department of Knowledge decides, and what the IB decides
paragraphs: Private schools in Ras Al Khaimah are regulated by the emirate's Department of Knowledge, which regulates private education in the emirate. Along with Sharjah's authority, it approves tuition fees, curricula, programmes, courses, activities and assessment methods. That is a broader remit than inspection, and it is routinely misunderstood by families who assume the regulator has a view on a TOK grade. It does not. The regulator licenses and oversees the school. The IB owns the course.

Getting this split straight saves a lot of wasted correspondence. A question about fees, about whether a campus is licensed to run the Diploma, or about a formal complaint against a school goes to the Department of Knowledge. A question about an internal TOK deadline, the exhibition mark the school awarded, or a predicted grade goes to the school. A question about the assessment rules themselves, including what counts as acceptable support, goes to the IB through the school's Diploma coordinator.

The federal layer sits underneath both. Private schools in the UAE are not obliged to follow a specific curriculum beyond Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies, but must adhere to the Ministry's general regulations. That is the rule behind the mandatory subjects every emirate requires, and it is the reason a Diploma student in Ras Al Khaimah carries hours that a Diploma student in Europe does not. Those hours are a real constraint on TOK time and are dealt with later on this page.

One more thing a regulator does not do, and nobody should imply otherwise: it does not accredit tutors or tutoring platforms. The licensing route for an operation with premises and staff is an educational services permit from the relevant authority. IB Gram is an online tutor-matching platform, holds no permit, accreditation, licence or endorsement from the Department of Knowledge, the Ministry of Education or the IB, and has no office in the UAE.

sections.heading: The two assessed tasks, the word limits, and the grade that can fail a Diploma
paragraphs: Theory of Knowledge is assessed on two pieces of writing and nothing else. The exhibition asks the student to pick one of the published internal assessment prompts, select three objects with a real-world context, and write a commentary of around 950 words explaining how each object connects to the prompt. It is marked by the school against a single holistic criterion and moderated by the IB. The essay is a maximum of 1,600 words answering one of six prescribed titles released for the session, and it is marked externally.

The weighting is worth knowing before a student decides which task to take seriously. The essay carries roughly two-thirds of the TOK grade and the exhibition the remaining third, which means the exhibition is the smaller task and the easier one to do well, because it is marked by a teacher who has told the class exactly what they want. Students who treat it as a warm-up and the essay as the real thing frequently give away the marks that were cheapest to collect.

Then there is the diploma arithmetic. TOK and the Extended Essay are graded A to E and combine on a matrix that awards up to three points towards the diploma total. More importantly, a grade E in either is a failing condition: a candidate can pass all six subjects and not receive the Diploma. In a small cohort this is the fact that changes behaviour fastest, because it reframes TOK from an optional intellectual exercise into a component with a floor underneath it.

What none of this rewards is fluency. A confident writer with a strong opinion and no knowledge question will score in the middle of the range and be surprised. The mark scheme asks for a sustained, clearly structured discussion of knowledge itself, with examples used to test arguments rather than to decorate them. That is a learnable discipline, which is precisely why coaching on TOK works better than coaching on most subjects: the student is not short of content, only of a method.

sections.heading: The exhibition: three objects, and why a Ras Al Khaimah object beats a borrowed one
paragraphs: Most weak exhibitions fail at the same point: the objects are generic. A student picks a smartphone, a newspaper and a photograph of a laboratory, and writes three paragraphs that could have been written by anyone anywhere. The mark scheme asks for objects with a specific real-world context, and specificity is the whole game. An object the student can describe precisely — where it is, who owns it, when it was made, what happened to it — gives them something to analyse. A category of object gives them nothing.

This is where living in Ras Al Khaimah is an advantage rather than a limitation. The emirate is full of objects with documented, local and genuinely unusual contexts. The pearling and fishing settlements along the northern coast towards Al Rams and Sha'am, the abandoned village at Al Jazirah Al Hamra, the mangrove reserve at Mina Al Arab, a ceramic tile from the emirate's industrial base, the terraced agriculture inland around Digdaga: each is a real thing a student can photograph, date and describe, and none of them will appear in another candidate's exhibition.

The discipline a coach brings here is mostly subtraction. The prompt is chosen first, because objects hunted before a prompt is settled tend to be forced into a connection afterwards, and an examiner can see the join. Then each candidate object is tested with three questions: can the student describe it specifically rather than generically, does it carry a knowledge claim rather than merely a story, and does it connect to the prompt in a way that needs explaining rather than merely asserting?

Word discipline is the last piece. Around 950 words across three objects is roughly 300 words each, which is not room for a history lesson. Students consistently spend 500 words on their favourite object and 150 on the third, and the third object is then marked as thin. A coach's most useful intervention is often arithmetic: three roughly equal sections, each with the object identified, its context given briefly, and the link to the prompt argued properly.

sections.heading: The essay: a prescribed title is a question about knowledge, not about the world
paragraphs: Six prescribed titles are released for each examination session, and a student chooses one. The single most common failure in TOK essays is answering the wrong question — not a different title, but the world-level version of the title the student was given. A title asking whether the methods of a discipline determine what it can know is a question about method and knowledge. Students answer it by writing about the discipline. Everything after that point is well-written and off-target.

The first sessions with a coach are therefore spent reading, not writing. All six titles get unpicked, even the five the student will not choose, because comparing them shows what kind of question this is. Each title gets broken into its terms: which words carry weight, which are doing decorative work, what the title presupposes, and what an answer would have to establish to count as an answer. A student who can state their title's demand in one sentence of their own words is ready to plan.

Then the structure. A strong TOK essay develops knowledge arguments and tests them against examples, usually drawn from two areas of knowledge handled in real depth. The weak alternative is five areas handled in outline, which reads as coverage rather than thought. Examples have to be specific enough to carry weight: a named historical dispute, a named study with a replication problem, a particular proof. Vague examples make an argument unfalsifiable, and an examiner has no way to credit it.

The 1,600-word ceiling then does useful work. It is not enough space for an introduction that restates the title, a conclusion that summarises the body, and five examples. Students who plan backwards from the limit — two arguments, two counter-positions, four precise examples, and a conclusion that actually concludes something — write better essays than students who write freely and cut. A coach reads one draft and gives written feedback on it, which is what IB rules permit, and the student makes every change themselves.

sections.heading: A Ras Al Khaimah school year with the TOK deadlines written in
paragraphs: A Diploma year in this emirate runs from late August or early September to late June, with a winter break in December, a spring break in March and Ramadan shifting earlier each year. Written out as months, that looks like plenty of time. Written out as usable weeks with the TOK deadlines, the Extended Essay submission, the mock window and the internal assessment deadlines in their real places, it is tight, and the tightness falls in a predictable pattern.

The pattern is this: DP1 is where TOK time exists and nobody uses it, and DP2 is where TOK deadlines arrive in the same six weeks as everything else. The exhibition is typically a DP1 task. The essay titles are released and the essay is written in DP2, and in most schools the internal TOK deadline sits close to the window where subject internal assessments and the Extended Essay are also due. A student who has not read their prescribed titles until that window will write their essay in the worst fortnight of the two years.

Counting backwards is the only plan that survives contact with a real school calendar. Find the school's internal TOK essay deadline. Subtract two weeks for the draft and the feedback the supervisor is permitted to give. Subtract four more for writing and redrafting. Subtract two more for choosing the title and building arguments. That lands the start date, and it is almost always earlier than the student expects and earlier than the school's formal launch of the task.

Ramadan deserves a line of its own, because families here plan around it and tutoring providers rarely acknowledge it. Sessions move to post-Iftar slots rather than being cancelled, which in practice protects two or three weeks of continuity that households often write off in advance. The same applies to the late-June finish and the long summer: a DP1 student who reads around their optional themes over the break starts DP2 with a vocabulary the rest of the class is still building. Confirm every IB date with your school's coordinator, because the IB sets and revises them and we do not publish them.

sections.heading: What Theory of Knowledge coaching costs in a market with almost no supply
paragraphs: Start at the bottom of the market, because that is where most parents start looking. Online tuition from a university student is advertised from AED 45 to 65 by EdFlik and from AED 33 to 52 by Tutopiya, which puts the budget tier somewhere between AED 45 and 150 an hour. For a routine subject that tier is a reasonable gamble. For Theory of Knowledge it usually is not, because the course is not content a bright undergraduate can read up on the night before; the whole task is a method of argument.

The next tier is a qualified subject teacher working online, roughly AED 150 to 300 an hour, with Unitors publishing IGCSE tuition from AED 150 and IB from AED 200. Above that sits the IB specialist band of AED 200 to 450 or more, where TutorChase quotes AED 270 and Bestimate's Dubai rate table reaches AED 450 and beyond. Premium named tutors go higher again, with BartyED publishing AED 650. TOK coaching generally prices in the specialist band because almost nobody teaches it privately.

For comparison, in-home one-to-one visits are quoted at AED 180 to 350 by Bestimate and AED 200 to 500 by independent home tutors. In Ras Al Khaimah that band is largely theoretical for TOK specifically: the number of people in the northern emirates who could teach the course well and would drive to Al Dhait on a Tuesday is very small. Monthly figures published in this market run around AED 799 for eight online sessions against AED 1,599 to 1,799 for four two-hour in-home sessions.

Those are market rates with their sources named, not an IB Gram price list, and that distinction matters because three of six ranking pages in this market publish no price at all while two quote in US dollars. TOK is also usually bought as a block rather than as an open-ended weekly commitment: a handful of sessions on the exhibition in DP1, then a run of sessions from title release to draft. Our own figure comes from the consultation after a free trial lesson.

sections.heading: Arabic, Islamic Education and the other hours a northern-emirates week already holds
paragraphs: A Diploma student in Ras Al Khaimah carries hours a Diploma student elsewhere does not, and any honest TOK plan has to be built around them. Private schools in the UAE are not obliged to follow a specific curriculum beyond Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies, but must adhere to the Ministry's general regulations. In practice that means Arabic, Islamic Education and social or moral studies sit alongside the six Diploma subjects, the Extended Essay, Theory of Knowledge and the activity requirement.

The emirate-level detail varies, and Dubai's requirements are the most publicly documented: KHDA requires separate classes by group, so that for Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies schools must organise separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs, with combined classes strictly prohibited because of different curriculum expectations and language of instruction. Dubai also calculates mandatory-subject time on a 40-minute lesson unit and advises that any mandatory subject lesson should last at least 25 minutes. Ras Al Khaimah families should confirm their own campus's arrangement with the school.

Why this belongs on a TOK page: those hours are the reason the honest answer to 'when can your child work on TOK' is narrower than a timetable suggests. A DP2 student with six subjects, Arabic, Islamic Education, a social studies requirement, an Extended Essay and a service commitment has perhaps two usable evening slots a week. A TOK plan that assumes four is a plan that will be abandoned in week three, and abandoning it in week three is how a grade C becomes a grade D.

There is an upside worth naming, too. Bilingual students carrying Arabic alongside an English-medium Diploma are sitting on first-hand material for the knowledge-and-language theme that monolingual candidates have to read about. A student who can describe a concept that does not translate cleanly between Arabic and English, and say precisely what is lost, has an example no textbook supplied. Several of the strongest exhibition objects we see from UAE students come straight out of that experience.

sections.heading: Where coaching stops and your child's own TOK work begins
paragraphs: TOK has the hardest honesty boundary in the Diploma, because the assessed product is an argument and an argument is the easiest thing in the world to hand over. The IB position is clear: the exhibition and the essay must be the student's own work, with one draft read and commented on by the supervisor. A coach can teach the method, test an argument, point at an example that will not bear weight, and read one draft. A coach cannot supply the thesis, restructure the essay, or draft any part of it.

In practice the line is easiest to hold by changing what a session does. A good TOK session is mostly questions. Why is that an object rather than a category? What would have to be true for your argument to be wrong? Which of your four examples is doing real work and which is decoration? Can you state the title's demand without using the title's own words? The student leaves with a list of things to fix and fixes them alone. If the session has produced text the student did not write, it has gone wrong.

Parents should also know what to ask a prospective coach, because this market contains people who will quietly cross the line. Ask directly what they will do with a draft, and listen for 'feedback' rather than 'sort it out' or 'polish it'. Ask whether they will provide a thesis. Ask whether their work would need to be declared to the school. A coach who cannot answer that last question is not someone to hire, and an agency offering finished essays is creating a malpractice finding for your child rather than solving a problem.

Declare the support. Schools expect to know about external tuition, and the student's own reflections and the supervisor's authentication both depend on an accurate picture. A student who has been coached properly has nothing to hide: the arguments are theirs, the examples are theirs, and the improvement is in how they were tested. That is the version worth paying for, and it is the only version that is safe.

process.title: Send what the school has issued
process.description: Before anything is booked, send the prompt list, the prescribed titles if they have been released, and whatever the student has written so far, even a paragraph. Reading the student's own material is a faster diagnosis than any conversation about how the course is going.

process.title: Free trial lesson with the named coach
process.description: The first session costs nothing, takes no card details and is taught by the coach who would continue. It works on the student's own prompt or title rather than on a generic exercise, and it ends with a written view on whether coaching is needed at all.

process.title: A written plan with the school's dates in it
process.description: The coach counts backwards from the school's internal deadline and sets out what each of the next few sessions will cover. The plan names the school's own dates, not generic ones, which is why we ask for them before the second session.

process.title: Blocks, not open-ended weekly tuition
process.description: TOK is usually bought as two blocks: the exhibition in DP1 and the essay in DP2. Sessions run on Gulf Standard Time and move to post-Iftar slots during Ramadan. We say when a block has done its work rather than extending it.

process.title: One draft, read and returned in writing
process.description: The coach reads one complete draft and returns written comments on the argument, the examples and the structure. The student makes every change themselves. Nothing is rewritten for them, and we will tell you if a request crosses that line.

whyPoints.title: Built for a small cohort, not a large one
whyPoints.description: In an emirate with a short list of IB campuses, a TOK student usually has one person to ask. An external coach is a genuine second interpretation of a prescribed title, available on an evening when the school's coordinator is marking the rest of the cohort's exhibitions.

whyPoints.title: Local objects instead of generic ones
whyPoints.description: A specific object with a documented context scores; a category of object does not. Ras Al Khaimah supplies unusually strong material, from the northern pearling settlements to the Mina Al Arab mangroves, and no other candidate in the session will have used it.

whyPoints.title: Rates quoted in dirhams, with sources named
whyPoints.description: Every figure on this page is a published market rate attributed to whoever published it. Three of six ranking pages in this market quote no price at all and two quote in US dollars, which is not a currency UAE families transact in.

whyPoints.title: The honesty boundary stated before you pay
whyPoints.description: A coach teaches the method, questions an argument and comments on one draft. We do not supply a thesis, restructure an essay or draft any part of the exhibition commentary, and we will tell you plainly if a request crosses that line.

whyPoints.title: The emirate's calendar taken seriously
whyPoints.description: Plans count backwards from your school's own internal deadline, work around Arabic, Islamic Education and social studies hours, and move to post-Iftar slots in Ramadan rather than pausing. A plan that ignores those is a plan abandoned by week three.

faqs.question: Who actually teaches Theory of Knowledge in a Ras Al Khaimah school?
faqs.answer: Usually a teacher whose main job is a subject — often English, History or a science — acting as TOK coordinator, sometimes supported by colleagues who each take an area of knowledge. In this emirate the Diploma cohorts are small, so that coordinator is typically the only person who has read all six prescribed titles closely, and they are also marking every exhibition in the year group. Ask at the next parents' evening who the coordinator is and how the course is timetabled. The answer tells you how much individual attention your child can realistically expect in school hours.

faqs.question: Can my child fail the IB Diploma because of Theory of Knowledge?
faqs.answer: Yes. Theory of Knowledge and the Extended Essay are graded A to E and combine on a published matrix that awards up to three points towards the diploma total. A grade E in either is a failing condition, which means a candidate can pass all six subjects and still not be awarded the Diploma. That is the fact that changes how seriously students take a course with no examination. It also means the exhibition, which is the smaller and school-marked task, is the cheapest place to protect the grade.

faqs.question: What object can my daughter use for the TOK exhibition in Ras Al Khaimah?
faqs.answer: Something she can describe precisely rather than a category of thing. A smartphone is a category; a specific phone with an owner and a history is an object. Ras Al Khaimah is unusually rich in usable material: the abandoned village at Al Jazirah Al Hamra, the pearling and fishing settlements towards Al Rams and Sha'am, the mangrove reserve at Mina Al Arab, a tile from the emirate's ceramics industry, the terraced agriculture inland around Digdaga. Choose the prompt first, then hunt objects, because objects found first tend to be forced into a connection afterwards.

faqs.question: How many words is the Theory of Knowledge essay and the exhibition commentary?
faqs.answer: The essay has a maximum of 1,600 words and answers one of six prescribed titles released for the session. The exhibition commentary runs to around 950 words covering three objects, which works out at roughly 300 words each. The second figure is the one students ignore: they spend 500 words on their favourite object and 150 on the third, and the third is then marked as thin. Plan three roughly equal sections, each identifying the object, giving its context briefly and arguing the link to the prompt.

faqs.question: Does the Ras Al Khaimah Department of Knowledge have anything to do with TOK?
faqs.answer: Not with the course. The Department of Knowledge regulates private education in the emirate and approves tuition fees, curricula, programmes, courses, activities and assessment methods at school level. The Theory of Knowledge mark scheme, the prescribed titles and the academic honesty rules are set by the IB and are the same everywhere. So fees and school licensing go to the regulator, internal deadlines and exhibition marks go to the school, and questions about assessment rules go to the IB through your school's Diploma coordinator.

faqs.question: How much should we pay for Theory of Knowledge coaching in Ras Al Khaimah?
faqs.answer: Market rates rather than ours. Budget online tutoring runs roughly AED 45 to 150 an hour, with EdFlik from AED 45 to 65 and Tutopiya from AED 33 to 52, which rarely suits a course that is a method rather than readable content. A qualified teacher online is about AED 150 to 300, with Unitors publishing IB from AED 200. The IB specialist band where TOK normally sits is AED 200 to 450 or more; TutorChase quotes AED 270. Premium named tutors reach AED 650, as BartyED publishes.

faqs.question: Can a tutor choose my son's prescribed title for him?
faqs.answer: A tutor can unpick all six titles with him, explain what each one demands and discuss which areas of knowledge each would need, and that is genuinely useful work. The choice itself should be his, because the essay has to be an argument he can sustain for 1,600 words and he is the one who knows which examples he can describe accurately. A title picked for a student by someone else tends to produce an essay written in borrowed language, which examiners notice. Declare any external support to the school.

faqs.question: My child says TOK is pointless. How do we get them to take it seriously?
faqs.answer: Two facts usually do it faster than persuasion. First, TOK and the Extended Essay together are worth up to three diploma points, which is often the difference between an offer and a near miss. Second, a grade E in TOK is a failing condition for the whole Diploma. Beyond the arithmetic, the course stops feeling pointless the moment a student finds one example they actually care about — a mistranslation, a disputed historical account, a study that would not replicate. A coach's first job is usually to find that example with them.

faqs.question: When in the Ras Al Khaimah school year does the TOK workload actually bite?
faqs.answer: In DP2, and in the same six weeks as everything else. The exhibition is normally a DP1 task and DP1 is where the time exists and nobody uses it. The essay is written in DP2, and in most schools the internal TOK deadline sits close to the window where subject internal assessments and the Extended Essay are also due. Count backwards from your school's own deadline: two weeks for draft feedback, four for writing, two for choosing a title. That start date is earlier than most students expect.

faqs.question: Is there anyone in the northern emirates who teaches Theory of Knowledge privately?
faqs.answer: Very few people, and that scarcity is the honest reason this page exists. TOK is not a timetabled subject with a department behind it, so the pool of people who have actually taught and marked it is small nationally and smaller still in Ras Al Khaimah, Umm Al Quwain and Fujairah. Published in-home rates of AED 180 to 500 an hour are largely theoretical for this course locally. IB Gram delivers TOK coaching one-to-one over live video; we do not send tutors to homes anywhere in the UAE.

faqs.question: Do Arabic and Islamic Education lessons leave time for TOK?
faqs.answer: They leave less than a timetable suggests, and a realistic plan has to account for it. Private schools in the UAE must cover Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies alongside their licensed curriculum. A DP2 student carrying six subjects, those mandatory hours, an Extended Essay and a service commitment has perhaps two usable evening slots a week. A TOK plan that assumes four will be abandoned by week three. There is an upside: bilingual students have first-hand material for the knowledge-and-language theme that monolingual candidates have to read about.

faqs.question: How is the Theory of Knowledge exhibition marked?
faqs.answer: The school marks it against a single holistic criterion and the IB moderates the marking. The commentary of around 950 words has to show, for each of three objects, what the object is in its specific real-world context and how it connects to the chosen prompt. Because the teacher marking it has told the class exactly what they want, the exhibition is the easier of the two tasks to score well on. Students who treat it as a warm-up give away the marks that were cheapest to collect.

faqs.question: Can TOK coaching happen over video if it is a discussion subject?
faqs.answer: It suits video better than most subjects. A TOK session is a shared document and an argument: the coach reads the student's plan or draft on screen, questions it, and the student annotates as they go. Nothing needs to be physically in the room. It also leaves a record of what was advised, which matters for a component where the honesty boundary is strict. The real variable is the student rather than the medium, so book the free trial and judge the match from the hour itself.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a TOK knowledge question and a normal essay question?
faqs.answer: A normal essay question asks about the world. A knowledge question asks how we come to know, how reliable that route is, and what happens when two routes disagree. The commonest failure in TOK essays is answering the world-level version of the title. If a title asks whether a discipline's methods determine what it can know, that is a question about method and knowledge; writing about the discipline is off-target however well it is written. Being able to restate the title's demand in your own words is the test.

faqs.question: How many sessions does a Theory of Knowledge student usually need?
faqs.answer: Fewer than a subject, and in two blocks rather than continuously. A typical pattern is three or four sessions on the exhibition in DP1, covering the prompt, the three objects and the word distribution, then a run of six to eight from the release of the prescribed titles to the school's internal draft deadline. After that, one session on the draft feedback is usually enough. Open-ended weekly TOK tuition across two years is rarely good value, and we will say when a block has done its work.

ras-al-khaimah/ib-dp-theory-of-knowledge.closingHeading: Bring the prompt list and the titles, and we will start there
ras-al-khaimah/ib-dp-theory-of-knowledge.closingBody: If you are looking for an IB DP Theory of Knowledge tutor in Ras Al Khaimah because nobody at home can explain what a prescribed title is asking, the quickest useful step is to send the prompt list, the titles if they have been released, and whatever your child has written so far. The free trial lesson then works on that material rather than on a generic exercise, and it ends with a written view on whether coaching is needed at all. Sessions run one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time, counted backwards from your school's own internal deadline.

ras-al-khaimah/ib-home-tutor.tutorsIntro: The tutors below teach single IB subjects at a named level over live video, one-to-one. None of them drives to a UAE address. Each will look at a piece of your child's own marked school work before a lesson plan is written, which is the part that decides whether the hour is useful.

intro.heading: The thing being bought is the travel
paragraphs: When a family in Ras Al Khaimah pays the premium for a home tutor rather than an online one, almost all of that premium buys travel. The teaching is the same teaching. What changes is that someone drives from wherever they live to your door, sits down, teaches, and drives back. Market rates for an in-home visit run roughly AED 180 to 500 an hour against AED 150 to 300 for a qualified subject tutor working online, and the gap is the car.

That is not an argument against it. Travel buys something real: an adult physically present, a student who cannot minimise the window, no device to manage, and a parent within earshot. For a Year 8 or Year 9 student who drifts the moment nobody is watching, that is worth money, and a family who has already worked that out should not be talked out of it by anyone selling an alternative.

What the travel also buys, unavoidably, is a smaller pool of tutors. Ras Al Khaimah is spread out. The distance from Al Nakheel to Mina Al Arab, or from Al Dhait to Al Marjan Island, is a genuine drive rather than a stroll between towers. The subset of tutors willing to make that drive for a single 7pm hour, four evenings a week, is far smaller than the subset who teach the subject — and it is selected for where they live, not for whether they have taught Higher Level Chemistry.

That trade is the whole of the decision, and it resolves differently by year group. For the Diploma years, where the shortage in this emirate is specialist subject depth rather than supervision, geography is the wrong filter. For the middle years, where the shortage is attention, geography may be exactly the right one. A parent who sees it in those terms will spend their money better than one comparing hourly rates.

IB Gram does not send tutors to homes anywhere in the UAE. Home visits are a service we offer only in India, and stating that here rather than at the bottom of a terms page is deliberate. Everything this page says about the local in-home market is written to be useful to a family who chooses that route regardless — what it costs, what to verify, what to ask about data and payment, and where in the house a session should actually happen.

The second half of the page covers the thing nobody writes about: whether a Diploma student has an hour spare at all. Six subjects, Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay, CAS and federally mandated UAE subjects already fill the week. Adding two tutored subjects to that timetable is the most common reason a tutoring plan is abandoned by November, and the fix is arithmetic rather than motivation.

ras-al-khaimah/ib-home-tutor.programmesIntro: Which IB stage your child is at changes the answer to the home-versus-online question more than anything else does. Supervision needs fall as independence rises; specialism needs climb as the course deepens. These four stages are where that crossover happens.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: Inquiry-led and internally assessed, with no terminal examination. At this stage physical presence is worth the most it will ever be worth: a seven-year-old reading aloud to an adult at the table is doing something a video call handles awkwardly. Most PYP requests resolve into a reading and number-fluency routine rather than subject tutoring.
programmes.countryNote: In Ras Al Khaimah the PYP cohort sits in a handful of campuses and the parent network is small, so recommendations circulate by word of mouth. That is an efficient way to find someone local and a poor way to verify them, which is why the doorstep checklist in this page matters most for this age group.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Eight subject groups, each assessed against four criteria on a 1-8 scale, finishing with the Personal Project. This is the stage where home tutoring most often earns its premium, because the common problem is sustained attention rather than missing expertise, and a generalist in the room beats a specialist on a screen for a distractible fourteen-year-old.
programmes.countryNote: MYP students in this emirate are frequently in a year group of fewer than thirty, which means criterion-based feedback is plentiful from the school and individual attention is scarce. A tutor's useful job here is teaching the student to read criterion language precisely rather than re-teaching content.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects with three normally at Higher Level, plus Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and CAS, graded 1-7 per subject with bonus points from the core. The crossover happens here: the student is old enough not to need supervision, and the content is deep enough that a tutor chosen for proximity is unlikely to have taught it.
programmes.countryNote: A Ras Al Khaimah Diploma student may be the only person in their year taking a given Higher Level subject. No classmate to compare an Internal Assessment draft with, no second teacher in the building to ask. That is a specialism shortage, and a shorter drive does not solve it.

programmes.name: Career-related Programme
programmes.description: DP courses combined with a career-related study and a core including a reflective project and personal and professional skills. Uncommon in the northern emirates. The DP courses inside it are assessed exactly as they are in the full Diploma, so subject support is identical work; the reflective project needs supervision instead.
programmes.countryNote: Where a family in Ras Al Khaimah is on this route, local tutoring provision for the career-related core is effectively absent, because the market has not seen enough of it. Process supervision over video is the practical option, and it is worth saying so rather than pretending otherwise.

ras-al-khaimah/ib-home-tutor.subjectsIntro: Below is the list a parent most often arrives with, written from the symptom side — what you are seeing at the kitchen table — rather than from the syllabus side, plus whether having the tutor physically present changes the answer.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: The symptom is usually a student who can follow a worked example and freezes on an unfamiliar question. That is method selection, and it is taught by working through problems with the student narrating their reasoning. Works equally well on a shared screen with a visible worked page; presence adds nothing here.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: The symptom is calculator dependence paired with weak interpretation — a correct regression and no idea what it means. Statistics is heavier than families expect. Screen sharing the calculator output alongside the question is actually easier remotely than peering at a handheld device together.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: The symptom is a student who revises diligently and loses marks on multi-step calculations and mechanism explanations. Fixing it requires someone who has marked that paper. One of the two scarcest Higher Level specialisms in the northern emirates, and the clearest case where a short drive is worth nothing.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: The symptom is confidence in the algebra and collapse on uncertainty treatment, graph interpretation and explaining what a gradient physically represents. Data-handling work is screen work by nature, with the student's own plotted graph on display and the criteria beside it.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: The symptom is full revision notes and mid-band extended responses. The cause is almost always terminology precision and answer structure rather than knowledge. Highly responsive to marked practice, and entirely format-independent.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: The symptom is strong commercial intuition and inaccurate diagrams. Axes, curve shifts and the new equilibrium carry explicit marks. The Internal Assessment commentaries need current articles and ruthless editing to a word limit, which is supervision rather than teaching.

subjects.name: Business Management
subjects.description: The symptom is a student who knows every framework and writes descriptively. Evaluation marks decide the grade, and they are earned by judging a decision for the named business in the case study. Teachable in a handful of sessions once the pattern is named.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: The symptom is a capable reader summarising instead of analysing. Marks sit in how meaning is made, not what the text says. Drafting and redrafting a paragraph together is one of the few things that genuinely benefits from a shared physical page, though a shared screen does most of it.

subjects.name: English B
subjects.description: The symptom is fluent conversational English and lost marks on text-type conventions, because a blog must read like a blog and a formal letter like a letter. Oral components benefit from recorded practice, which is easier remotely than in a room.

subjects.name: Arabic A and Arabic B
subjects.description: Arabic runs both as an IB language and as a federally mandated school subject. Arabic A assumes first-language fluency and literary analysis; Arabic B is the acquisition route. Arabic A at the higher grades is a thin specialism across the emirates, which rules out selection by postcode.

subjects.name: Theory of Knowledge
subjects.description: The symptom is a bright student who cannot work out what is being asked, because the course rewards argument rather than content. The useful intervention is a sustained conversation in which the student defends a claim and has it questioned, which is format-neutral and rarely available at a small school.

subjects.name: Extended Essay
subjects.description: The symptom is a question too broad to answer in 4,000 words and a method that will not survive contact with the data. Support means narrowing, planning and interrogating the student's own draft. Authorship stays with the student and the school supervisor signs for it.

ras-al-khaimah/ib-home-tutor.regionsIntro: This is the part of the in-home decision that no tutoring page publishes. Ras Al Khaimah's residential areas are genuinely far apart, and a tutor's willingness to visit depends on where they live relative to you. These notes describe the practical travel picture families report.

regions.name: Al Nakheel
regions.note: Central and the best-served area for in-home visits, because most locally advertising tutors are either here or can reach it quickly. If you live here the in-home market is a real market rather than a shortlist of one.

regions.name: Mina Al Arab
regions.note: Waterfront and expanding, with a meaningful drive back to the centre at school-run hours. Tutors frequently quote a higher rate or decline a single hour here, because the round trip consumes more time than the lesson.

regions.name: Al Marjan Island
regions.note: Reclaimed, low-density and at the end of a causeway, so there is no passing traffic and no short alternative route. The least practical address in the emirate for a weekday in-home session, and the one where video changes the most.

regions.name: Al Hamra Village
regions.note: Gated and coastal, with security procedures that add minutes at each end of a visit. International-school families cluster here, so word-of-mouth tutor recommendations circulate, but the pool remains small.

regions.name: Al Dhait
regions.note: Large, established and relatively central across Al Dhait North and South, with the emirate's second concentration of tuition provision. In-home visits are viable and this is the most price-sensitive part of the market.

regions.name: Khuzam
regions.note: Close to school provision with short school runs, which makes it the one area where a 4.30pm in-home start is genuinely achievable rather than theoretical. Afternoon slots here do not collide with the evening commute.

regions.name: Al Qusaidat
regions.note: Northern and largely local-resident, with Arabic A and mandatory-subject requests more common than Higher Level science. Tutors who cover those subjects are scarce and rarely the nearest person.

regions.name: Julphar
regions.note: Dense mixed-use near the old town, with apartment households and limited visitor parking. Twice-weekly shorter sessions fit this area better than a single long block, in either format.

regions.name: Seih Al Uraibi
regions.note: Inland, part industrial, with long commutes to the coastal schools. Sessions realistically start after 7.30pm, which is past the point most in-home tutors will take a new booking.

regions.name: Al Mamourah
regions.note: Quiet and residential, with many households commuting towards Umm Al Quwain or Sharjah. A tutor needing to arrive by 6pm is usually the constraint that breaks the arrangement here.

schoolClusters.city: Ras Al Khaimah schools and their catchment
schoolClusters.note: Because the emirate's international schools are concentrated in a few locations, the school run and the tutoring slot compete for the same stretch of road at the same hour. That overlap, more than the hourly rate, decides whether an in-home arrangement lasts a full term.

schoolClusters.city: Where families look when a subject is not offered
schoolClusters.note: A subject combination that the local schools do not run turns into a relocation, a boarding conversation or a long daily drive south. It is the background to many tutoring enquiries from this emirate, because tutoring is the cheaper way to hold a position rather than move.

modes.title: In-home visit from a local tutor
modes.description: A tutor travels to the house for a fixed block, typically 60 to 120 minutes, and the rate includes their travel. Available in the Ras Al Khaimah market at roughly AED 180 to 500 an hour. Best for younger students and for households that want an adult physically present. IB Gram does not provide this in the UAE.

sections.heading: What a home visit in Ras Al Khaimah actually costs once travel is in the number
paragraphs: An in-home hour in this market sits at roughly AED 180 to 500, against AED 150 to 300 for a qualified subject tutor online and AED 45 to 150 at the university-student end. Those figures come from providers' own published pages and from Bestimate's 2026 Dubai tutoring cost table; they describe the market rather than IB Gram's pricing, and Ras Al Khaimah generally sits a little below Dubai in the middle of the range.

The headline rate is not the whole cost, and the differences are where families get caught. Minimum block length is the first: many in-home tutors will not take a single hour at a distant address, so the real commitment is two hours. Travel loading is the second: a rate quoted for Al Nakheel is often quoted again, higher, for Mina Al Arab or Al Marjan Island. Cancellation terms are the third, and they matter more for in-home work because a cancelled visit costs the tutor a round trip they cannot recover.

Monthly packages are widespread and hard to compare. Figures circulating in this market include AED 799 a month for eight online sessions and AED 1,599 to 1,799 a month for four two-hour in-home sessions. Divide every package by total teaching minutes before comparing, because a four-session package of two-hour visits and an eight-session package of one-hour lessons contain the same teaching time at very different prices.

For context on the wider cost picture, KHDA confirmed in May 2026 that private school fees in Dubai would not rise for the 2026-27 academic year under Dubai's second economic incentives package. Ras Al Khaimah sets its own fee approvals through the Department of Knowledge, so that does not apply here, but it is the benchmark most UAE families have in mind when they budget.

sections.heading: The drive is the constraint nobody writes down
paragraphs: Tutoring pages describe cities as though every address were interchangeable. In Ras Al Khaimah they are not. Al Marjan Island sits at the end of a causeway with no passing traffic. Mina Al Arab is a genuine drive from the centre. Seih Al Uraibi is inland and the coastal schools are a commute away. A tutor's decision about whether to take your booking is made on that map, not on your child's subject.

The practical effect is a selection problem. The tutors who will drive to a distant address for a weekday evening hour are a small subset, and membership of that subset is determined by where they live and what else they have booked. If the two people in the emirate who have taught Higher Level Chemistry both live on the wrong side of the city, no amount of budget produces a visit. The market has a hard ceiling that an hourly rate cannot lift.

Timing compounds it. A 6pm in-home session requires the tutor to leave at perhaps 5.20pm and to be driving home at 7.15pm, which is two and a half hours of their evening for one billable hour. That is why minimum blocks exist, why travel loading exists, and why in-home tutors in spread-out emirates cluster their bookings geographically rather than by subject. None of this is bad faith; it is the arithmetic of driving.

The honest conclusion is that the in-home market works well for central addresses and middle-years subjects, and works poorly for peripheral addresses and specialist Diploma courses. A family in Khuzam looking for Year 9 maths support is well served. A family on Al Marjan Island looking for Higher Level Chemistry is not, and should know that before spending three weeks finding out.

sections.heading: The doorstep checklist: what to verify before anyone comes in
paragraphs: If you do engage a local tutor, there is a short list of things to establish before the first visit, and none of it is awkward to ask. The first is the permit. An individual providing private tuition in the UAE needs the MoHRE private tutor work permit, introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023. It is granted free of charge for two years. Because it costs nothing, there is no legitimate reason for a working tutor not to hold one, which makes the question entirely fair.

Eligibility is broad: teachers registered in government or private schools, employees in the government and private sectors, unemployed individuals, school students aged 15 to 18, and university students. MoHRE's own service page for it is titled Issuance of a New Work Permit - Private Tutor Licensing, lists no fees and a two-working-day completion time, and applications go through the MoHRE smart app, website and e-services system. Individuals tutoring without a permit are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws. No fine schedule is published, so disregard any specific figure you see quoted online.

The second item is the school boundary. Abu Dhabi's professional-ethics rules prohibit private and charter school staff from paid private tutoring of students enrolled at their own school, and the permit's code of conduct also bars serving students affiliated with the tutor's own school. If the person standing on your doorstep teaches your child during the day, that is the wrong arrangement regardless of how good they are.

The third is data, and it is the item every provider skips. Lead forms and tutor onboarding collect personal information about a minor. UAE Federal Decree-Law No. 45 of 2021 on Personal Data Protection governs that. A reasonable provider can tell you what it collects, why, where it is stored and how to have it deleted, and keeps a privacy policy reachable from every page. A tutor or platform that wants your child's school, year group, grades, photograph and home address with no stated purpose is collecting more than the job needs.

Confirm the tutor does not teach at your child's own school

sections.heading: Where in the house the session should happen, and why it matters
paragraphs: This is a practical question with a practical answer, and it applies to both formats. Sessions work in a semi-public room — a dining table, a study with the door open, a family room — rather than a bedroom. For an in-home visit that is a safeguarding norm worth holding to without needing a reason. For a video session it matters for a different reason: a student at a dining table with a parent passing through behaves differently from a student in bed with a laptop.

The physical setup does more work than families expect. A hard surface the student can write on, in view of the camera for online work, converts a passive hour into an active one. The single biggest difference between a video session that works and one that does not is whether the student is writing. A tutor who cannot see the student's working is reduced to talking, and talking is the least effective thing a tutor does.

Household traffic is the second variable. Younger siblings, a television in the same room, a doorbell during a 90-minute block — these are the real reasons sessions underperform, and they are fixable without spending anything. Agreeing with the household that the dining table is unavailable between 7pm and 8.15pm on Mondays and Wednesdays does more for outcomes than switching tutors.

For an in-home visit there are two further items worth settling: where the tutor parks, particularly in Julphar and other apartment areas with limited visitor parking, and whether a gated community like Al Hamra Village requires pre-registration of a visitor. Both have caused more cancelled first sessions than any academic factor.
bullets: Semi-public room, door open, never a bedroom
A writing surface in view of the camera for video sessions
A household agreement about that room and that hour
Parking and gate access settled before the first in-home visit

sections.heading: Does a Diploma student even have an hour spare?
paragraphs: Before buying any tutoring, it is worth doing the arithmetic on the week. A Diploma student carries six subjects, three of them at Higher Level with extra content and in most sciences an extra paper, plus Theory of Knowledge, a 4,000-word Extended Essay, CAS commitments, and the UAE's federally mandated subjects. Private schools are not obliged to follow a specific curriculum beyond Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies, but must adhere to the ministry's general regulations, so those hours are in the timetable.

KHDA's guidance for Dubai gives a sense of the scale of the mandatory load: instructional time is calculated on a 40-minute lesson unit, schools may vary lesson length provided the total weekly time is met, and it is advised that any mandatory-subject lesson runs at least 25 minutes. Schools must organise separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs in Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, with combined classes strictly prohibited. Ras Al Khaimah sits under its own Department of Knowledge rather than KHDA, but the federal requirement behind these subjects applies across the country.

Add it up and the picture is usually clear: there is room for one tutored subject, comfortably, and for two only if something else gives. The most common way a tutoring plan fails in this emirate is not a bad tutor — it is three subjects booked in September and two quietly abandoned by November, with the family concluding that tutoring does not work. It worked; the timetable did not.

The planning move is to pick the subject where the next stage depends on the grade, or where the gap is widest, and fix that one properly. A subject moved two grades is worth more than three subjects nudged, and it leaves the student with enough week left for the Extended Essay they also have to research and write themselves.

sections.heading: When proximity helps, and when it is simply irrelevant
paragraphs: Having a tutor in the room helps with a specific, identifiable set of problems: attention, pace, physical practice, and the reassurance of a younger student. It helps a Year 8 student who stops working when nobody is watching. It helps a child who needs someone to physically point at the line of working where the error happened, though a shared screen does most of that. It helps a family who wants to overhear the session.

It is irrelevant to a different, equally identifiable set: knowledge of the specific paper, familiarity with the published assessment criteria, the ability to mark against a scheme and attribute every lost mark, and the supply of a scarce specialism. Those are properties of the tutor, not of the tutor's location. A family paying a travel premium for a subject where specialism is the binding constraint is paying for the wrong thing.

The crossover usually sits somewhere in Years 10 and 11. Below it, supervision tends to dominate. Above it, expertise does. That is not a rule and it varies by child — some Year 13 students need an adult in the room and some Year 8 students work better alone than observed — but it is the right default to argue from, and it maps onto what Ras Al Khaimah families actually report.

sections.heading: Ramadan, the school year, and the hours that quietly disappear
paragraphs: A tutoring plan written in September and never revisited meets three predictable disruptions, and in-home arrangements survive them less well than remote ones because a cancelled visit is harder to replace than a cancelled call. Planning for them in advance is the difference between a plan that runs for a year and one that collapses in March.

The first is Ramadan. School hours shorten, household routines shift to the evening, and the usual pattern is for sessions to move to the early afternoon or to a post-Iftar slot. Shorter and more frequent works better than long blocks. For a Diploma student in their final year this period matters disproportionately, because the examination session does not move, so momentum lost in Ramadan has to be recovered in the weeks immediately before the papers.

The second is the Internal Assessment cluster. Across six subjects the internal deadlines bunch, and in the fortnight either side of that cluster a student has no capacity for anything else. The sensible response is to pause weekly subject tutoring deliberately and use those hours for Internal Assessment supervision instead, then resume. Paying for sessions nobody has energy to attend is the most avoidable waste in this market.

The third is the examination session itself. Cambridge and Pearson publish their timetables and dates; for the IB, we do not publish a session or results date on this page, because the IB's own site could not be confirmed directly and a date a family plans around has to come from the school's IB coordinator. Ask for the school's own examination calendar in writing in the autumn term and build backwards from it.

sections.heading: The academic-honesty line, and why it applies at home too
paragraphs: A tutor sitting at your dining table with your child's Internal Assessment open on the laptop is in exactly the same position as one on a video call, and the rule is the same. Assessed work must be the student's own. A tutor may teach the underlying skill, read the published criteria aloud with the student, discuss a plan the student has made, ask questions about a draft the student has written, and give feedback the student then acts on. A tutor may not author any part of what is submitted.

Physical proximity makes the line easier to cross by accident, which is worth naming. A tutor with a pen in hand, trying to be helpful at 9pm the night before a deadline, can end up editing rather than questioning. The protection is procedural rather than moral: the student types, the tutor asks, and the tutor never has the document open on their own device in editing mode.

Operators in this market sell finished Internal Assessments, with completed work advertised at around AED 3,750. The consequence of using one falls on the candidate as an IB malpractice matter, not on the seller. The school supervisor signs an authenticity declaration, so the record has to be honest. A family that understands where the line is cannot be sold across it.

Materials follow the same principle. Syllabus documents, past papers, mark schemes, grade-boundary tables and subject guides belong to the IB, Cambridge and Pearson, and are referenced and linked from their official sources rather than redistributed. A tutor who arrives with a memory stick of restricted material is telling you how they operate generally.

sections.heading: What we actually do, and how to start
paragraphs: IB Gram matches Ras Al Khaimah families to IB subject specialists who teach one-to-one over live video, in Gulf Standard Time, with late-evening slots because nobody is driving anywhere. Home visits are a service we run only in India. If you have read this page and concluded that an adult in the room is what your child needs, the local market supplies it and the checklist above is what to verify before you engage someone.

If specialist subject depth is the binding constraint, the sequence is short. A ten-minute conversation about the actual problem: subject, level, what the last marked work showed, and the date you are working towards. Then a free trial lesson, one subject, with no payment and no card details, so the format is judged on your own child rather than on a claim. Then a written plan naming two priority topics, the session slot and the dates of the timed papers.

Scarcity gets a straight answer. Higher Level Chemistry, Higher Level Physics and Arabic A are thin specialisms in UAE evening hours. Where the match will take a week, we say a week. Where a specialist exists only at a time that does not suit your household, we say that and let you decide rather than substituting a generalist and hoping.

And the plan is reviewed against evidence at six weeks: a comparable paper re-sat and marked the same way, two breakdowns compared, and a decision to increase, reduce, switch subject or stop. Stopping because the problem is fixed is a legitimate outcome, and a provider who will not name it is selling rather than advising.

process.title: Decide which constraint is binding
process.description: Work out whether the problem is supervision, structure or expertise before shopping for anyone. Supervision points to an adult in the room. Structure points to a centre class. Expertise on a specific paper points to a specialist, wherever they live. Buying the wrong one is how families conclude tutoring does not work.

process.title: Get one marked paper, free
process.description: Ask the school for the subject's assessment outline and have your child attempt one real past paper under timed conditions. Marked against the published scheme with the loss attributed by question, that single document separates a content gap from a technique gap and tells you which kind of help to buy.

process.title: Verify before you engage anyone
process.description: For a local in-home tutor: the MoHRE private tuition work permit, confirmation they do not teach at your child's school, written cancellation terms, and a clear answer on what personal data about your child is collected and how to delete it. For any provider, a reachable privacy policy.

process.title: Free trial lesson over live video
process.description: One full one-to-one session on the subject you actually need, at no cost and with no card details. Expect the student to attempt real questions and the tutor to finish by naming the two specific things to fix. An hour of tutor explanation tells you almost nothing about the match.

process.title: Protect the hour in the household
process.description: Agree which room and which hour, twice a week, and make it unavailable to everyone else. A writing surface in view of the camera, no television, no doorbell duty. This costs nothing and does more for the outcome than changing tutors, in either format.

process.title: Review at six weeks against a re-marked paper
process.description: The student re-sits a comparable paper, marked the same way, and the two breakdowns are compared. The decision that follows is more sessions, fewer, a different subject or none. We will tell you which the evidence supports, including when the answer is none.

whyPoints.title: We price the travel rather than hide it
whyPoints.description: The in-home premium in this emirate is mostly the round trip, and the minimum blocks, travel loadings and cancellation terms that follow from it are set out here with sources. A family who understands what they are paying for can decide properly, including deciding against us.

whyPoints.title: Selection by subject, not by postcode
whyPoints.description: Over live video the pool is everyone who teaches that course and is free that evening, rather than everyone willing to drive to Al Marjan Island at 6.30pm. For Higher Level sciences and Arabic A in this emirate, that is the difference between a specialist and whoever is nearest.

whyPoints.title: Late slots, because nobody is driving
whyPoints.description: Sessions run in Gulf Standard Time with slots after 7.30pm available, which is past the point most in-home tutors will accept a booking from Seih Al Uraibi or Al Mamourah. Removing the journey removes the scheduling constraint that breaks most arrangements here.

whyPoints.title: A stated position on your child's data
whyPoints.description: We can say what is collected about a student, why, and how to have it removed, and a privacy policy is reachable from every page. UAE Federal Decree-Law No. 45 of 2021 governs this, and a provider that cannot answer the question is collecting more than the work requires.

whyPoints.title: Finite engagements with a review date
whyPoints.description: Internal Assessment blocks end when the school's deadline does. Pre-session intensives end on a fixed date. Weekly work is reviewed at six weeks against a re-marked paper. An open-ended arrangement with no measure is how families pay for momentum rather than progress.

whyPoints.title: Coverage limits said out loud
whyPoints.description: Higher Level Chemistry, Higher Level Physics and Arabic A are thin in UAE evening hours. Where the match takes a week, we say a week; where only an awkward slot exists, we describe it and let you choose. Nobody else in this market publishes a coverage limit at all.

faqs.question: Can I get a home tutor in Ras Al Khaimah for IB Diploma subjects?
faqs.answer: There is a local in-home market and it does cover IB subjects, though thinly at Higher Level. Rates run roughly AED 180 to 500 an hour with travel priced in, minimum blocks of two hours are common at distance, and the pool available to you is determined by where tutors live relative to your address. IB Gram does not provide home visits anywhere in the UAE; that service exists only in India. We deliver one-to-one over live video instead, which is why we can match on who has taught the course rather than on who is willing to drive to Mina Al Arab on a Tuesday.

faqs.question: What does a home tutor charge per hour in Ras Al Khaimah, and is travel charged on top?
faqs.answer: Market figures put an in-home hour at roughly AED 180 to 500, against AED 150 to 300 for a qualified subject tutor working online. Travel is usually inside the rate rather than itemised, which is why the same tutor often quotes differently for Al Nakheel and for Al Marjan Island — the second journey costs them more evening. Expect a minimum block, frequently two hours, and expect late cancellations to be charged in full because the trip cannot be recovered. Those figures come from providers' own published pages and Bestimate's 2026 Dubai rate table, not from us.

faqs.question: How long is the drive from Al Nakheel to Mina Al Arab for a 7pm session?
faqs.answer: Long enough to change the economics rather than long enough to be impossible. The practical issue is not the single journey but the round trip: a tutor leaving home at around 6.20pm to teach at 7pm is driving back after 8pm, which is roughly two and a half hours of their evening for one billable hour. That is the reason minimum blocks and travel loadings exist in this emirate, and the reason a peripheral address has a much smaller pool of willing tutors than a central one. Al Marjan Island, at the end of a causeway with no passing traffic, is harder again.

faqs.question: Is a home tutor better than online for my son in Year 9?
faqs.answer: Quite possibly, yes. At Year 9 the binding constraint is usually attention rather than specialist expertise, and physical presence is genuinely effective for a student who stops working the moment nobody is watching. The content at this stage is within the reach of a strong generalist, so the smaller local pool costs you little. The calculation inverts a couple of years later, when Higher Level content arrives and the thing you need is someone who has marked that specific paper. Deciding year by year rather than once is the right approach, and for Year 9 the local market is a reasonable first stop.

faqs.question: What should I check before letting a private tutor into the house?
faqs.answer: Four things, none of them rude to ask. First, the MoHRE private tuition work permit, introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023 and granted free of charge for two years — since it costs nothing, there is no reason for a working tutor not to hold it. Second, that they do not teach at your child's own school, which the permit's code of conduct addresses. Third, written cancellation and late-arrival terms. Fourth, what personal data about your child they or their platform collect, why, and how to have it deleted. Keep a payment record rather than paying cash with no receipt.

faqs.question: What personal information is it reasonable for a tutoring provider to collect about my child?
faqs.answer: Enough to do the work and no more: name, year group, subject, level, and the marked work you choose to share. A provider asking for a photograph, a full home address, a grade history and school details with no stated purpose is collecting beyond the task. UAE Federal Decree-Law No. 45 of 2021 on Personal Data Protection governs personal data here, and a serious provider can tell you what it holds, why, where it is stored and how to have it removed, with a privacy policy reachable from every page. If nobody can answer that question, it is a reasonable reason to walk away.

faqs.question: Does a home tutor in Ras Al Khaimah need a licence?
faqs.answer: An individual providing private tuition needs the MoHRE private tutor work permit. MoHRE's own service page is titled Issuance of a New Work Permit - Private Tutor Licensing, lists no fees and a two-working-day completion time, and applications are made through the MoHRE smart app, website and e-services system. Eligible applicants include registered school teachers, government and private-sector employees, unemployed individuals, school students aged 15 to 18 and university students. Those tutoring without a permit are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws. No fine schedule is published, so ignore any specific amount quoted online. A tutoring business with premises is a separate regime entirely.

faqs.question: Can two of my children share one home tutoring session?
faqs.answer: Tutors in the local market frequently agree to it, usually at a modest premium over the single rate rather than double, and for siblings in the same subject and close in level it can work well. The honest caveat is that it stops being one-to-one. A shared session teaches to the midpoint of two students, which is a small version of the problem a group class has, and it does not work at all when one child is two years ahead. Where the two children have genuinely different gaps, two shorter separate sessions deliver more than one long shared one, in either format.

faqs.question: Where in the house should a tutoring session actually happen?
faqs.answer: A semi-public room with the door open — a dining table, a study, a family room — and not a bedroom. That holds for an in-home visit as a safeguarding norm and for a video session for a practical reason: a student at a table with a parent passing through works differently from one with a laptop in bed. Provide a hard writing surface, in view of the camera for online sessions, because the single biggest predictor of a useful hour is whether the student is writing. Settle parking and gate registration in advance for an in-home visit in a gated community.

faqs.question: How many hours a week does an IB Diploma student realistically have spare?
faqs.answer: Fewer than families assume. Six subjects, three normally at Higher Level, Theory of Knowledge, a 4,000-word Extended Essay, CAS and the UAE's federally mandated Arabic, social studies and Islamic studies all sit inside the week before any tutoring is added. In practice there is comfortable room for one tutored subject and room for a second only if something else gives. Booking three in September and quietly abandoning two by November is the most common failure in this market, and it gets mistaken for tutoring not working. Pick the subject where the grade matters most and fix that one properly.

faqs.question: Do mandatory Arabic and Islamic Education lessons affect the tutoring timetable?
faqs.answer: Yes, in two ways. They occupy timetable hours alongside the IB courses, so the school day is fuller than the subject list suggests, and they generate their own homework and assessment. KHDA's framework for Dubai gives the scale: instructional time is calculated on a 40-minute lesson unit, with any mandatory-subject lesson advised to run at least 25 minutes, and separate classes are required for Arabs and non-Arabs in Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies. Ras Al Khaimah sits under its own Department of Knowledge, but the federal requirement behind these subjects applies nationally, so plan the week with them in it.

faqs.question: Can home tutoring continue through Ramadan in Ras Al Khaimah?
faqs.answer: It can, with the timing moved rather than the plan abandoned. School hours shorten and household routines shift towards the evening, so sessions commonly go to the early afternoon or to a post-Iftar slot, and shorter more frequent sessions work better than long blocks. In-home arrangements are more fragile in this period because a moved visit has to fit a tutor's driving schedule as well as your household's. For a final-year Diploma student the period matters disproportionately, since the examination session does not move. Agree the Ramadan pattern a fortnight ahead rather than improvising weekly.

faqs.question: What happens if the tutor cancels or arrives late?
faqs.answer: That depends entirely on terms you should agree in writing before the first session, and it is the most commonly skipped conversation in the in-home market. Ask what happens if the tutor cancels, if you cancel, if the tutor arrives twenty minutes late, and whether the time is made up or forfeited. In-home arrangements are more exposed in both directions because every session carries a journey. For video sessions the usual practice is rescheduling rather than forfeiting, since there is no unrecoverable trip, but it should still be written down rather than assumed.

faqs.question: Which IB subjects does having the tutor physically present actually help with?
faqs.answer: Presence helps where the constraint is attention, pace or reassurance — most commonly in the middle years, and in any subject for a student who disengages when unobserved. It helps marginally with handwritten mathematics, where pointing at a line of working is natural, though a shared screen covers most of that. It is essentially irrelevant where the constraint is expertise: Higher Level sciences, Internal Assessment criteria literacy, Theory of Knowledge argument, Extended Essay supervision and scarce languages such as Arabic A. Those depend on who the tutor is rather than where they are sitting, and selecting by distance removes most of the available pool.

faqs.question: Why does IB Gram not offer home visits in the UAE?
faqs.answer: Because the model would select tutors by driving distance, and in an emirate like this one that is the wrong criterion. A Diploma cohort here can be a dozen students, with perhaps three taking a given Higher Level subject, so the number of locally resident specialists is very small and those who exist are generally employed full time. Matching on availability over live video instead means the constraint becomes who has taught the course, not who lives nearby. Home visits remain a service we offer in India, where the density and the market are different. For UAE families everything is delivered one-to-one over live video.

faqs.question: Is it cheaper to pay monthly or per session for home tutoring?
faqs.answer: Compare on total teaching minutes before comparing on price, because packages in this market are structured to make that difficult. Figures circulating include AED 799 a month for eight online sessions and AED 1,599 to 1,799 a month for four two-hour in-home visits — the same eight hours at very different prices. Monthly commitments usually reduce the per-hour cost and remove your flexibility to stop at six weeks, which matters if the plan turns out to be wrong. For a first engagement, a small number of sessions with a review date generally beats a month bought in advance.

ras-al-khaimah/ib-home-tutor.closingHeading: Decide what you are buying before you buy it
ras-al-khaimah/ib-home-tutor.closingBody: If what you need is an adult in the room, the Ras Al Khaimah market supplies that and this page tells you what it costs, which areas it reaches and what to verify on the doorstep. If what you need is someone who has taught Higher Level Chemistry and can mark your child's paper against the published scheme, distance is the wrong way to choose and the local pool is too small to choose from. Start with the free step either way: ask the school for the assessment outline and get one timed paper marked. A free trial lesson over live video is available after that, one subject, with no payment taken.
